Title: itwinai: Enabling Scalable AI Workflows on HPC for Digital Twins in Science
Text:
itwinai: Enabling Scalable AI Workflows on HPC for Digital
Twins in Science
Matteo Bunino1,∗, Jarl Sondre Sæther1,∗∗, Anna Elisa Lappe1,∗∗∗, Maria Girone1,∗∗∗∗, and
Kalliopi Tsolaki1,†
1European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), Esplanade des Particules 1, Geneva
Abstract. itwinai is a Python library designed to facilitate scalable AI work-
flows on High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems. By abstracting com-
plex engineering tasks, it reduces overhead and enables seamless scaling of AI
models across diverse infrastructures. Deployed on HPC systems, such as Jülich
and Vega, itwinai allows users to switch between distributed machine learning
(ML) frameworks, including PyTorch DDP, DeepSpeed, and Horovod, through
a unified interface. The library integrates mechanisms for profiling compu-
tational efficiency, tracking key metrics, such as GPU utilization and power
consumption, and optimizing hyperparameters at scale. Additionally, it pro-
vides transparent offloading of compute-intensive tasks from the cloud to HPC
systems and supports model and pipeline parallelism to accommodate large-
scale models. A continuous integration and deployment pipeline ensures re-
producibility and compatibility across environments. In the interTwin project,
itwinai has been utilized in physics and climate research use cases, demonstrat-
ing its potential to enhance sustainability and computational efficiency. Its inte-
gration with leading scientific computing centers highlights its role in advancing
AI-driven digital twins and addressing large-scale scientific challenges.
1 Introduction
Digital twins (DTs) are dynamic virtual representations of physical systems that integrate
real-time data and ML to enable simulation, prediction, and optimization. Unlike tradi-
tional simulations, DTs continuously synchronize with their physical counterparts, allowing
for adaptive modeling and improved predictive accuracy. The interTwin project [1] builds
around this concept by developing the prototype of a Digital Twin Engine (DTE) that ensures
interoperability, performance, portability, and scientific reliability. Using High-Performance
Computing (HPC) and cloud infrastructures, interTwin facilitates the development and de-
ployment of domain-specific DTs across diverse scientific applications.
A key component of interTwin is itwinai [2], a Python library designed to streamline
scalable AI workflows on HPC systems. By abstracting the complexity of distributed ML,

itwinai enables researchers to efficiently scale their models across heterogeneous comput-
ing environments. The library supports multiple distributed training frameworks, including
PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) [3], DeepSpeed [4], and Horovod [5], allowing
users to optimize their workflows with minimal engineering effort. In addition, it provides
mechanisms for profiling computational efficiency, monitoring key system metrics, and inte-
grating hyperparameter optimization (HPO) techniques to enhance model performance.
itwinai also supports offloading compute-intensive tasks from cloud-based environ-
ments to HPC systems, enabling researchers to access specialized hardware, such as large
pools of GPUs. Its capabilities have been validated in physics and climate research applica-
tions, demonstrating its potential to enhance scientific computing workflows. By addressing
the challenges of scalable AI deployment, interTwin and itwinai contribute to advancing
the role of digital twins in scientific discovery and technological innovation.
2 The interTwin Digital Twin Engine
The interTwin project develops the prototype of a modular Digital Twin Engine (DTE) [6],
designed to support diverse scientific applications through a layered architecture composed
of thematic modules, core modules, and infrastructure services. These components respec-
tively encapsulate domain-specific functionality, horizontal core capabilities for digital twin
development, and foundational services for computing and data federation. This modular ar-
chitecture, introduced in detail in [7], supports the flexibility and scalability of the DTE and
guides the structure of the following sections.

2.1 DTE thematic modules
Thematic modules are domain-oriented building blocks that implement scientific workflows
tailored to specific research areas. These modules are developed in collaboration with domain
experts and act as practical demonstrators of how digital twin concepts can be instantiated in
real scientific use cases. Within interTwin, thematic modules include those for high-energy
physics, radio astronomy, climate analytics, Earth observation, and hydrology.
For example, the high-energy physics module supports tasks such as fast simulation and
event generation using generative models. The radio astronomy module addresses noise char-
acterization and source detection through distributed machine learning techniques. The cli-
mate analytics module focuses on impact assessment using downscaling and event detection
on large-scale datasets. The Earth observation module implements data processing chains for
flood monitoring based on Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data and openEO [8] processes.
Hydrological modelling workflows integrate real-time data from satellite sources to support
early warning systems. These modules are designed to interoperate with core DTE services,
enabling reuse of capabilities such as AI orchestration and data fusion.
2.2 DTE core modules
Core modules [7] provide shared capabilities that are reusable across scientific domains. They
support essential digital twin functions such as workflow composition, AI model develop-
ment, metadata harmonization, and validation.
One of the core modules is itwinai, primarily developed by CERN, which manages the
AI workflow and method lifecycle (see Section 3). It supports distributed ML training, hyper-
parameter optimization, and modular integration of AI toolkits tailored to HPC environments.
Other core modules include tools for composing complex workflows using directed acyclic
graphs, data fusion pipelines that integrate heterogeneous sources, and real-time data analyt-
ics frameworks that rely on serverless computing models. Validation and uncertainty tracing
mechanisms ensure that the DTE components maintain scientific rigor and reproducibility.
2.3 DTE infrastructure
Infrastructure services within the DTE provide the backbone for executing digital twin ap-
plications at scale across federated computing and data environments. These services enable
seamless access to heterogeneous resources and ensure interoperability between institutional
platforms.
Federated data management handles cataloging, caching, and standardized access to dis-
tributed datasets. Compute infrastructure supports the orchestration of tasks across HPC,
cloud, and hybrid environments with dynamic resource provisioning. The orchestration mod-
ule uses performance telemetry data to optimize scheduling and execution strategies. Au-
thentication and authorization services integrate institutional credentials and trust anchors to
enable secure and federated user access.
Together, these components form a cohesive and extensible platform that supports the
development and operation of digital twins in scientific research.
3 itwinai: AI Workflow and Method Lifecycle Management
The itwinai module is a comprehensive solution for AI workflow and method lifecycle
management developed by CERN, in collaboration with Forschungszentrum Jülich (FZJ). It
provides a robust framework for researchers, data scientists, and software engineers involved

3.1 Core Functionalities
The core functionalities of itwinai address key challenges in the development and deploy-
ment of scalable AI workflows for scientific applications. These include mechanisms for
efficient distributed training, automated hyperparameter optimization, and robust model life-
cycle management. Together, these components enable researchers to leverage HPC envi-
ronments with minimal engineering overhead while ensuring reproducibility, performance
tracking, and seamless workflow integration.
3.1.1 Distributed Training
itwinai provides a streamlined interface for distributing existing machine learning code
across multiple GPUs and compute nodes, enabling researchers to leverage the performance
benefits of HPC systems with minimal modification to their code. A general overview of dis-
tributed machine learning concepts is provided in Figure 3. The framework supports widely
adopted backends such as PyTorch Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), DeepSpeed, Tensor-
Flow’s distributed strategies, and Horovod. This provides a flexible and reliable foundation
for scalable training. Users can seamlessly switch between these frameworks through a uni-
fied configuration interface, which facilitates the rapid evaluation and tuning of distributed
training workflows. This level of abstraction also simplifies the benchmarking of different
distributed training approaches on the same model and dataset, making it easier to compare
their scalability and energy efficiency.

3.1.2 Hyperparameter Optimization
A key feature of itwinai is its advanced support for hyperparameter optimization (HPO).
Manually tuning hyperparameters is often time consuming and may lead to suboptimal re-
sults. Leveraging the Ray Tune library [9], itwinai automates this process, enabling ef-
ficient exploration of large hyperparameter spaces using state-of-the-art optimization algo-
rithms. This capability facilitates the development of more robust and accurate scientific
models, while lowering the barrier for researchers to perform tuning tasks on HPC systems.
An overview of the HPO workflow implemented in itwinai is provided in Figure 4.
3.1.3 Model Lifecycle and Logging Abstractions
itwinai provides an abstraction layer over widely used logging frameworks, such as
MLFlow [10], Weights & Biases [11], TensorBoard [12], and yProvML [13], allowing users

sign simplifies workflow integration and enables switching between different backends with-
out modifying user code. Additionally, itwinai integrates with MLFlow’s model registry
to support model versioning and lifecycle management, including tracking, promotion, and
deployment of models. These capabilities enhance reproducibility and collaboration by con-
solidating key aspects of ML experiment tracking in a flexible and extensible framework.
3.2 Technical Innovations and Integrations
In addition to its core functionalities, itwinai introduces a range of technical innovations
that enhance its portability, efficiency, and usability across heterogeneous computing envi-
ronments. These developments focus on enabling seamless integration with cloud and HPC
infrastructures, supporting reproducible software deployment, and providing detailed insights
into performance metrics. The following components illustrate how itwinai supports cross-
infrastructure compatibility and facilitates optimization of distributed training workflows.
3.2.1 Cross-Infrastructure Compatibility
Recognizing the importance of reproducibility and cross-infrastructure compatibility,
itwinai integrates a continuous integration and deployment pipeline to build and test con-
tainers automatically. This ensures researchers have access to up-to-date, tested software
for deployment across both cloud and HPC environments. Additionally, the library enables
transparent offloading of compute-intensive tasks from the cloud to HPC systems through
integration with interLink [14]. In collaboration with Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare
(INFN) [15] and UPV [16], this capability was demonstrated using OSCAR [17], where AI
inference on Vega HPC was triggered for real-time data ingestion.
3.2.2 Performance Monitoring and Optimization
itwinai provides functionality for measuring the scalability of key metrics when distribut-
ing training across multiple nodes. The library quantifies communication overhead by com-
paring the time spent on communication with the time spent on computation. Additionally,
the library probes the GPU at regular intervals, aggregating data to inform the user about
GPU utilization and power consumption. This probing is performed in a non-intrusive man-
ner, ensuring that efficiency is not compromised. Finally, the library provides insights into
how wall-clock time varies with different numbers of compute nodes and distributed training
frameworks. Some examples of results from these analyses can be seen in section 4.
Monitoring these performance metrics enables scientists to optimize their models by
identifying bottlenecks in computation and communication, ensuring efficient resource uti-
lization.
By analysing GPU utilization and power consumption, researchers can make
sustainability-conscious decisions, such as balancing energy efficiency with model perfor-
mance. Additionally, detecting unexpected slowdowns in wall-clock time or unusually high
communication overhead can help diagnose suboptimal configurations or erroneous imple-
mentations in distributed training setups. This insight ensures that models run efficiently
while optimizing the utilization of computational resources.
4 Experiments
Experiments were conducted on two digital twin (DT) use cases to evaluate the scalability
and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) capabilities of the framework.

The first use case, Noise in the Virgo Gravitational Wave Interferometer, focuses on sim-
ulating noise in gravitational wave detection. The simulated noise is subtracted from the
measured signal to facilitate the identification of gravitational wave events. This use case,
developed by the Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN), is referred to as Virgo in this
submission.
The second use case, Drought Early Warning in the Alps, aims to predict water availabil-
ity in the Alpine region. In the context of climate change and the observed decline in water
resources, early drought prediction has become increasingly important. A DT is employed
to better capture and forecast such patterns, supporting preparedness for potential drought
events. This use case, developed by Eurac Research, is referred to as EURAC in this submis-
sion.
Results from an HPO experiment on the EURAC use case are presented in Figure 5. The
experiment included 28 trials using a random search strategy, along with one trial using hy-
perparameters manually selected by a domain expert. Several random trials outperformed the
expert configuration in terms of validation loss, with the best trial achieving a 74% reduction
in validation loss.
Scalability analysis results are shown in Figure 8. The computation fraction varies across
frameworks when scaling over multiple GPUs. In particular, torch-ddp exhibits higher fluc-
tuation in this run, which may be attributed to bottlenecks in the use case code or to external
factors during training, such as network congestion or other transient system conditions.
Additional insights are provided in Figure 7, which illustrates a general increase in energy
consumption accompanied by a decrease in GPU utilization across all frameworks. This
pattern suggests that the scaling behavior of the use case code may be suboptimal, potentially
due to excessive inter-worker communication overhead.
Finally, Figure 6 shows that DeepSpeed achieves more consistent scaling performance,
while the other two frameworks demonstrate greater variability.
5 Conclusions
The interTwin project establishes a modular and extensible architecture for the development
of scientific digital twins, using high-performance computing and federated infrastructures to
enable scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable applications. Central to this architecture
is the itwinai module, which offers comprehensive support for AI workflow management
and method lifecycle operations in distributed environments.
The capabilities of itwinai have been validated through collaborative efforts with scien-
tific institutions, including the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC) [18],
Eurac Research [19], and INFN [15], across diverse domains such as climate modeling and
gravitational wave data analysis. These use cases have demonstrated the module’s ability to
efficiently orchestrate distributed training workflows, perform large-scale hyperparameter op-
timization, and manage model provenance and reproducibility within HPC-enabled pipelines.
Ongoing developments focus on extending the framework’s applicability to large-scale AI
models through support for model and pipeline parallelism, thereby accommodating emerg-
ing requirements in scientific machine learning, such as transformer models. These efforts
are aimed at ensuring the continued relevance of the platform for increasingly complex and
data-intensive applications.
In summary, interTwin and itwinai provide a robust foundation for the advancement of
digital twin technologies in scientific research. Future work will further explore integration
with continual learning strategies, automated validation mechanisms, and cross-domain in-
teroperability, thereby contributing to the broader goal of enabling trustworthy and efficient
digital twin ecosystems.
